cues.text: So, the task I gave you both was to choose an article about a small-scale research project.
cues.speaker: Tutor

cues.text: Yes ...
cues.speaker: Leela and Jake

cues.text: You were then required to try to reproduce the research procedures in your own context ... i.e. try it out for yourselves.
cues.speaker: Tutor

cues.text: Yeah ... and that’s what we’ve done.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: Great. So I’d like you to tell me a bit about the article and why you chose it.
cues.speaker: Tutor

cues.text: Well, the article’s written by two university lecturers who had started using crosswords to help their students revise terminology for exams .
cues.speaker: Leela

cues.text: And the crosswords were designed and set on computers.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: And we selected the article because ... well it seemed an accessible topic, even though we weren’t familiar with the technique ... you know ... using IT to design crosswords for higher education.
cues.speaker: Leela

cues.text: That’s a good reason. So these lecturers wanted to see how well this innovation was received by their students?
cues.speaker: Leela

cues.text: Yes.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: So how did you go about reproducing the research?
cues.speaker: Tutor

cues.text: Well, we drew up a list of terms from one of our own modules ... and designed a crossword for revising these terms.
cues.speaker: Leela

cues.text: Then we asked our classmates to try out the crossword and give us feedback, you know, their opinions, on how they felt about using the technique.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: Was it easy to find participants?
cues.speaker: Tutor

cues.text: It wasn’t easy at first. But then we convinced them that by taking part in the research they were actually benefiting themselves by preparing for an exam which is coming up later this term.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: And it worked!
cues.speaker: Leela

cues.text: Good. So how did you find out what the students thought about doing the crosswords?
cues.speaker: Tutor

cues.text: A questionnaire. The original article used a two-page long questionnaire. There were lots of excellent questions on it but the whole section on difficulties using IT is now obsolete ... old-fashioned even, even though it had only been written a couple of years ago.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: So you designed a shorter version?
cues.speaker: Tutor

cues.text: Yeah. Then we sent it to the forty students by email and got twenty-eight replies. I was taken aback by the fact that everybody we talked to thought this was a good return! I mean the responses were well written, you know, people had taken a lot of care, but I was really disappointed with the low numbers.
cues.speaker: Leela

cues.text: Yes, an important lesson to learn for an apprentice researcher .
cues.speaker: Tutor

cues.text: Yeah.
cues.speaker: Leela and Jake

cues.text: So what results did you get?
cues.speaker: Tutor

cues.text: Well, basically the responses were extremely positive. The students said that doing the crossword on a computer helped them really focus on the work in hand and not be distracted, which is something that commonly happens with other ways of doing of revision.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: Yeah ... that was really clear. But something that struck me was that ‘having fun’ hardly featured in their responses ... nor did anything to do with spelling of hard words ... which I thought would be an obvious benefit.
cues.speaker: Leela

cues.text: No? OK ...
cues.speaker: Tutor

cues.text: Respondents also said that doing the crossword hadn’t really increased their general motivation to study but that it had highlighted the gaps in their memory so they knew what further work was necessary.
cues.speaker: Leela

cues.text: Right ... So how did your findings tally with those of the original researchers?
cues.speaker: Tutor

cues.text: There were lots of similarities but ...
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: There were probably two main differences. We found that more males than females liked the technique, whereas the original study found the reverse.
cues.speaker: Leela

cues.text: Also, our respondents said they wouldn’t mind doing a crossword as a final official exam ... whereas in the original study students said they would hate doing it even if it meant having a shorter test.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: But of course both sets of respondents said they’d be interested in doing more crosswords for informal purposes, revision and so forth.
cues.speaker: Leela

cues.text: Right, so let’s have a think about the whole project and what you’ve learned from doing it.
cues.speaker: Tutor

cues.text: Well ... it was very time consuming!
cues.speaker: Leela

cues.text: Yeah! And I don’t think we managed that aspect very well.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: It could have been worse ... I mean we didn’t have a lot of data so we didn’t have to spend ages processing it. And of course, we’d already done a course on numerical data processing so there wasn’t much new there.
cues.speaker: Leela

cues.text: Yeah, that’s true. Anyway, I think we designed our questions well so that they gave us manageable data.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: Yeah, it really helped having the original study to guide us, as it were ... and that helped us see what a good research instrument is ....
cues.speaker: Leela

cues.text: what a good questionnaire should be like.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: Absolutely - we got a lot from that. But when we were writing up the project, I’m not sure whether we’ll know how to acknowledge the work of the original study ... you know, our referencing.
cues.speaker: Leela

cues.text: No ... that’s something we’ll both have to work on in the future.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: Actually that part’s been great, finding ways to share and support another person.
cues.speaker: Leela

cues.text: That’s the real plus from the project ... learning ways to do that.
cues.speaker: Jake

cues.text: Well, it’s obviously been very successful ...
cues.speaker: Tutor
